subject: Critical Thinking
title: Reversible vs. Irreversible Decisions
description: A fast breakdown of Reversible vs. Irreversible Decisions for builders.

hook.text: Jeff Bezos divides decisions into 'one-way doors' and 'two-way doors'. Each deserves different treatment.

buildup.text: Two-way doors: decide fast, iterate, learn. The cost of reversal is low. Most daily decisions are two-way.

discovery.text: One-way doors: decide carefully, gather evidence, consult broadly.

twist.text: The mistake most people make: treating two-way doors like one-way doors.

climax.text: The opposite mistake is worse: treating one-way doors like two-way doors.

punchline.text: Reversible? Decide fast. Irreversible? Decide wisely.

quiz.question: How should 'two-way door' decisions be treated?
options: Decided quickly, since they can be reversed easily

details.summary: Jeff Bezos distinguishes Type 1 decisions (irreversible, high-stakes) from Type 2 decisions (reversible, low-stakes). Most decisions are Type 2 and should be made quickly, but organizations often treat every decision as Type 1.
details.whyItMatters: Treating reversible decisions with the same caution as irreversible ones causes analysis paralysis and wastes time on choices that can easily be undone.
takeaways: Reversible decisions should be made quickly and adjusted
Most decisions are more reversible than they feel in the moment

faq.question: How do you tell whether a decision is truly irreversible?
faq.answer: Ask: can I undo this with reasonable cost and effort? Hiring someone is largely reversible. Selling your house and moving to another country is much less so. True irreversibility is rarer than it seems.

faq.question: Why do organizations tend to over-deliberate on reversible decisions?
faq.answer: Fear of mistakes, blame culture, and the illusion that more analysis reduces uncertainty. In reality, for Type 2 decisions, the cost of delay often exceeds the cost of a suboptimal choice that can be corrected.
